Earth may have repeatedly slipped outside the Sun’s protective bubble
Research highlighted by NASA on 24 August 2026, with the underlying heliosphere review published in the August 2026 volume of Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics.

NASA-funded researchers reconstructed the Sun’s recent journey through the Milky Way and found that it likely encountered dense interstellar cold clouds at least three times in the past 14 million years. During these encounters, surrounding gas may have compressed the heliosphere — the bubble carved out by the solar wind that normally shields the planets — to smaller than Earth’s orbit, temporarily leaving Earth directly exposed to the interstellar environment. The modeled encounters line up with unusual isotopes found in deep-sea sediments, Antarctic material, and lunar samples, and could have altered atmospheric chemistry, radiation exposure, and perhaps ancient climate.

Earth’s long-term environment is influenced not only by its orbit and the Sun’s activity, but also by the Sun’s motion through the Galaxy. That adds an external variable to questions about planetary climate, radiation, habitability, and potentially the evolution of life.

Roman launches to map the dark universe and hunt thousands of exoplanets
NASA announced Roman's successful launch on 30 August 2026, selected within the 15-day freshness window.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched successfully on 30 August 2026 and is now traveling toward the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. Roman will combine infrared sensitivity and image sharpness comparable to Hubble with a field of view roughly 100 times larger, allowing it to survey enormous areas of the sky far more quickly. Its main science goals include measuring how dark energy has influenced cosmic expansion, mapping dark matter through gravitational lensing, and discovering thousands of exoplanets. NASA says the observatory will spend roughly three months traveling and commissioning before science operations begin, with first public images expected in early 2027.

Roman is designed to turn questions about dark energy, dark matter, and exoplanet populations into survey-scale measurements, giving astronomers statistical samples far larger than Hubble or Webb can efficiently produce over the same sky area.

Hubble uncovers the Milky Way’s earliest confirmed major merger
Published by NASA Hubble on 17 August 2026 and selected within the 15-day freshness window.

Hubble observations have helped identify the Milky Way’s earliest confirmed major merger, involving the Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles system. The finding shows that accreted stars from external galaxies were already important during the Galaxy’s earliest growth.

The finding pushes the Milky Way’s confirmed merger history about 1.8 billion years farther back and shows that accreted stars from external galaxies were already important during the Galaxy’s earliest growth.

S301: the fastest known star in the Milky Way may reveal Sagittarius A*’s spin
Published by ESO on 19 August 2026 and selected within the 15-day freshness window.

S301 is the fastest known star in the Milky Way and passes exceptionally close to Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the Galactic Centre. Its orbit may be measurably altered by relativistic effects caused by the black hole’s rotation, offering astronomers a new way to probe that spin.
S301 passes so close to Sagittarius A* that relativistic effects from the black hole’s rotation should measurably alter its orbit, creating a practical new test of strong-field gravity.
